source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with decode. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: single-node decode-heavy serving of a dense ~9B model in bf16 on A30-class GPUs (24 GB HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical HBM bandwidth), continuous batching scheduler, paged KV cache.

Failure mode 1 - HBM bandwidth starvation at low batch size (mechanism). Each decode step reads the entire weight set once regardless of how many sequences are in flight: ~18 GB for 9B params in bf16. At an achieved ~70% of 933 GB/s = ~650 GB/s, the weight streaming alone costs 18/650 s = ~28 ms/step, i.e. ~36 tok/s per sequence and that number is nearly independent of batch size until KV traffic dominates. So decode with B=1 wastes almost all FLOPs: the GEMMs degenerate into GEMVs with arithmetic intensity ~2 FLOP/byte, far below the ~200+ FLOP/byte ridge point of the device. Boundary condition: this holds only while B * bytes_per_token_KV_read << weight_bytes. Once the aggregate KV read per step approaches the weight bytes, further batching stops being free and the step time grows roughly linearly with B.

Failure mode 2 - KV cache capacity collapse / preemption thrash (trade-off). The obvious fix for mode 1 is a larger batch, but KV cache is the binding constraint. For a 9B model with 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16: per token per layer = 2 (K,V) * 8 * 128 * 2 B = 4096 B, times 40 layers = ~164 KB/token. With ~6 GB left for KV after weights and activations on a 24 GB card, that is ~38k tokens total, e.g. 18 concurrent sequences at 2k context. Exceeding it forces the scheduler to preempt and either swap KV to host over PCIe or recompute prefill, which shows up as multi-hundred-millisecond TPOT spikes and p99 blowups while mean throughput still looks fine. Boundary condition: the collapse is triggered by the tail of the length distribution, not the mean; a scheduler admitting on average context length will thrash as soon as a few long sequences arrive.

Trade-off statement: throughput (large B) and tail latency (small B, headroom for long sequences) are traded against each other through a single shared resource, KV cache bytes.

Falsifiable predictions: (a) sweeping B from 1 to 16 at fixed context should leave per-step time nearly flat until KV traffic is comparable to weight traffic; (b) driving KV utilization above ~90% should produce preemption counters > 0 and a p99 TPOT regression of >2x while p50 barely moves.

Evidence to collect: per-step time vs B curve, nvidia-smi / DCGM dram_active and achieved HBM GB/s, engine counters for preempted/swapped requests, KV blocks used vs total, p50/p95/p99 TPOT.

Rollback gate: if p99 TPOT exceeds the SLO by >20% or preemption count per minute is nonzero at steady state, reduce max_num_seqs / KV utilization target and re-measure before keeping the change.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with decode. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: dense decoder-only model served with continuous batching; measurements on the deployment's own hardware, no vendor numbers assumed.

Failure mode 1 - tensor-parallel decode becomes collective-latency bound (mechanism). Splitting a model across TP=N shrinks per-GPU weight bytes by N, which helps mode-1 bandwidth starvation, but inserts two all-reduces per transformer layer on the critical path of every single decoded token. For 40 layers that is ~80 collectives per token. Each all-reduce of hidden_size elements is tiny (e.g. 4096 * 2 B = 8 KB per rank), so it runs entirely in the latency regime of NCCL, not the bandwidth regime: cost is dominated by kernel launch plus link latency, typically single-digit to low-tens of microseconds on NVLink and substantially worse over PCIe or across nodes. 80 * 20 us = 1.6 ms/token of pure communication. Boundary condition: TP scaling of decode only pays off while (weight_bytes / N) / achieved_BW still exceeds the per-token collective cost; past that crossover, adding GPUs increases TPOT.

Failure mode 2 - speculative decoding trades wasted compute for latency and can regress (trade-off). Draft-then-verify decoding proposes k tokens with a small draft model and verifies them in one target forward pass. Mechanism: it converts k bandwidth-bound target steps into one, so speedup ~ accepted_length / (1 + draft_cost_ratio). Boundary condition: it only wins when the target model is bandwidth bound, i.e. at small batch. Under high load with large B the target is already near compute-saturated, acceptance-rate variance adds jitter, and the extra draft forwards plus rejected-token compute reduce aggregate throughput. Reported single-stream speedups do not transfer to loaded multi-tenant serving.

Falsifiable predictions: (a) TPOT vs TP degree will be U-shaped, with the minimum at a TP degree that decreases as interconnect latency increases; (b) speculative decoding's throughput gain will cross zero as offered load rises, and the crossing point is measurable.

Evidence to collect: NCCL kernel time share from a profiler (nsys or torch profiler), per-layer all-reduce time, NCCL_DEBUG topology confirming NVLink vs PCIe path, TPOT vs TP sweep, acceptance-rate distribution and tokens/s vs QPS with and without speculation.

Rollback gate: revert to the lower TP degree or disable speculation if p50 TPOT regresses at all or aggregate tok/s at target QPS drops by more than 5% in a 30-minute A/B.

source_user: Explain how decode interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: bf16 dense model, paged-attention engine (vLLM-class), single node, steady-state decode-dominated traffic.

Latency. Time-per-output-token (TPOT) in decode is set by a serialized chain per token: weight read from HBM, KV read from HBM, attention and MLP kernels, plus any tensor-parallel collectives. Concrete mechanism: at batch B, step_bytes ~= W + B * L_ctx * bytes_per_token_KV, where W is the full weight set. TPOT ~= step_bytes / achieved_HBM_BW + collective_and_launch_overhead. Because W is paid once per step and not once per sequence, single-stream latency is essentially a hardware constant for a given model and dtype; no scheduler tuning fixes it. Only weight quantization (e.g. bf16 -> int8/fp8 halving W), TP sharding, or speculative decoding move it.

Throughput. Aggregate tokens/s = B / TPOT. Since TPOT is nearly flat in B while KV traffic is small relative to W, throughput grows almost linearly with B in that regime. This is why continuous batching is the single highest-leverage decode optimization: it keeps B high by admitting new requests at token granularity instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish.

Memory. Memory is what caps B and therefore throughput. KV bytes per token = 2 * n_kv_heads * head_dim * n_layers * dtype_bytes. GQA/MQA reduce n_kv_heads and are the main reason long-context serving is feasible. Paged KV cache eliminates internal fragmentation from pre-reserving max_seq_len per request, typically raising achievable concurrency substantially versus contiguous allocation.

Boundary condition. The linear-throughput regime ends when B * L_ctx * bytes_per_token_KV approaches W. Past that point attention reads dominate, step time grows with total live tokens, and adding concurrency buys throughput at strictly proportional latency cost. Long contexts reach this crossover at small B; short contexts may never reach it before KV capacity runs out.

Falsifiable prediction: plotting TPOT against total live KV tokens (not against request count) should yield a curve that is flat then linear, with the knee at total_KV_bytes ~ W.

Evidence to collect: TPOT and tok/s vs B at fixed and mixed context lengths, KV blocks used, achieved HBM bandwidth, preemption/swap counters, p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT.

Rollback gate: keep a concurrency setting only if it holds p99 TPOT within SLO for at least one full traffic peak with zero preemptions; otherwise revert.

source_user: Explain how decode interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: production serving with mixed prefill and decode traffic; SLOs stated separately for TTFT and TPOT.

Interaction with latency. Decode latency is not just the model step; it is the step plus queueing behind prefill. Concrete mechanism: a single long prefill (e.g. 8k tokens) is compute bound and can occupy the GPU for tens to hundreds of milliseconds. If the scheduler runs it as one monolithic batch, every decoding sequence stalls for that entire duration, producing a TPOT spike visible only in p99. Chunked prefill fixes this by splitting the prefill into token-budgeted chunks co-scheduled with decode, bounding the stall to one chunk. Disaggregated prefill/decode (the design behind NVIDIA Dynamo and Mooncake-style architectures) goes further by placing the two phases on separate GPU pools and transferring KV over the fabric.

Interaction with throughput. Co-scheduling raises decode TPOT slightly but removes head-of-line blocking, so it usually improves p99 far more than it costs p50. Disaggregation lets each pool be provisioned for its own bottleneck - prefill pool sized on FLOPs, decode pool sized on HBM bandwidth and KV capacity - which is why it wins at scale.

Interaction with memory. Disaggregation makes KV transfer explicit: the prefill pool's KV must reach the decode pool. Over RDMA/RoCE with GPUDirect RDMA the transfer is GPU-HBM to GPU-HBM without host bounce buffers. Bytes moved = L_prompt * bytes_per_token_KV; for ~164 KB/token and a 4k prompt that is ~670 MB per request, which at 200 Gb/s (~25 GB/s achievable) is ~27 ms - comparable to the prefill itself. Boundary condition: disaggregation only pays when KV transfer time is materially less than recomputing prefill on the decode node; short prompts and thin fabrics fall on the wrong side of that inequality.

Falsifiable prediction: for a given fabric bandwidth there is a prompt-length threshold below which disaggregation increases end-to-end TTFT; that threshold is measurable by sweeping prompt length.

Evidence to collect: p99 TPOT with and without chunked prefill, scheduler stall histograms, KV transfer bytes and wall time, ib_write_bw and nv_peer_mem/dmabuf confirmation that GDR is actually active, TTFT vs prompt length for both topologies.

Rollback gate: revert disaggregation if measured KV-transfer p99 exceeds 30% of the TTFT budget or if GDR cannot be confirmed active (silent fallback to host staging roughly doubles the cost).

source_user: Explain how decode interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: quantized-weight decode under evaluation; hardware and dtype support verified rather than assumed.

Latency. Decode step time is approximately (weight_bytes + KV_bytes) / achieved_HBM_bandwidth. Concrete mechanism: quantizing weights from bf16 to fp8 or int8 halves weight_bytes and, in the bandwidth-bound low-batch regime, roughly halves TPOT. This is a bandwidth effect, not a FLOPs effect - the win appears even on hardware with no native low-precision tensor cores, provided dequantization is fused into the GEMM epilogue and does not itself become the bottleneck. Boundary condition: if the kernel dequantizes to a full-precision buffer in HBM before the GEMM, total traffic increases and latency gets worse, not better.

Throughput. Freed HBM (e.g. 18 GB -> 9 GB for a 9B model) converts directly into KV cache capacity, raising the achievable concurrent batch. Because throughput ~ B / TPOT and both terms improve, the aggregate gain can be superlinear relative to the naive expectation. KV cache quantization (fp8 KV) attacks the other term, extending the flat region of the TPOT-vs-B curve.

Memory. The binding limit shifts: with quantized weights, KV usually becomes the dominant consumer, so the next optimization is GQA, KV quantization, or prefix/paged sharing rather than more weight compression.

Falsifiable prediction: fp8 weights should reduce single-stream TPOT by close to the weight-byte ratio (within kernel overhead), and should NOT materially help at large batch where KV traffic dominates. If the observed speedup is uniform across batch sizes, the model was not actually bandwidth bound and the explanation is wrong.

Evidence required: TPOT vs B for both dtypes, achieved HBM GB/s, nvidia-smi memory breakdown, kernel-level profile confirming fused dequant, and an accuracy check - task-level evaluation on held-out data, not perplexity alone, since perplexity is insensitive to the tail behaviour quantization damages.

Rollback gate: revert quantization if any tracked task metric drops beyond a pre-registered threshold (e.g. >1 point absolute on the primary eval), or if p99 TPOT fails to improve; performance wins do not license silent quality regressions.

source_user: Explain how decode interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: multi-node decode across nodes connected by RoCEv2; NIC and GPU topology known from lspci/nvidia-smi topo -m.

Latency. When decode is sharded across nodes (TP or PP crossing the node boundary), every token's collectives traverse the network. Concrete mechanism: with GPUDirect RDMA the NIC DMAs directly into GPU BAR1/HBM, skipping a host bounce buffer and cutting one memcpy plus one PCIe traversal per direction; without it, NCCL stages through pinned host memory and per-collective latency rises measurably. Because decode issues ~2 collectives per layer per token, a few microseconds of added latency multiplies by ~80 into a directly visible TPOT increase. Boundary condition: GDR requires the GPU and NIC to sit under the same PCIe root complex (or an acceptable switch path) and the nvidia_peermem/dmabuf path to be loaded; if the topology is cross-socket, GDR can be slower than staging, which is why NCCL has thresholds and can disable it.

Throughput. RoCE is lossless only if PFC and ECN/DCQCN are configured consistently end to end. Mechanism: without ECN marking, incast from many decode ranks causes buffer buildup, PFC pause frames propagate back through the fabric, and throughput collapses in bursts. This appears as periodic TPOT spikes uncorrelated with request load - a network problem masquerading as a serving problem.

Memory. Cross-node decode does not reduce KV per token; it only distributes it. Pipeline parallelism adds per-stage KV plus bubble sensitivity, and at decode's batch-of-one-token-per-sequence the pipeline bubble is proportionally largest.

Falsifiable predictions: (a) disabling GDR (NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=0) should raise TPOT by a measurable, repeatable amount if GDR was active; if TPOT does not change, GDR was never active. (b) TPOT spikes should correlate in time with PFC pause counters on the ToR switch.

Evidence required: nvidia-smi topo -m, NCCL_DEBUG=INFO showing the selected transport, ib_write_lat/ib_write_bw baselines, switch PFC/ECN counters, nccl-tests all_reduce_perf at the message size decode actually uses (kilobytes, not megabytes).

Rollback gate: do not cross the node boundary for TP unless a same-message-size nccl-test shows collective latency below the budget implied by the TPOT SLO divided by 2 * n_layers; otherwise keep the model within one node.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether decode helps a serving workload. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Goal: decide whether a proposed decode-path change (e.g. enabling continuous batching, raising max_num_seqs, or turning on chunked prefill) actually helps this serving workload. Assumption: one candidate change per experiment; everything else pinned.

1. Pre-register the decision rule. Primary metric: sustained output tokens/s at the highest QPS that still meets p99 TPOT <= X ms and p99 TTFT <= Y ms. Declaring "throughput improved" without holding latency fixed is the most common way these measurements lie.

2. Fix the workload. Replay a captured production trace, not synthetic uniform prompts - decode behaviour is driven by the input/output length distribution, and a fixed 512/128 benchmark hides KV-capacity failures entirely. Record the distribution so the run is reproducible.

3. Pin the environment. Same engine commit, model weights hash, dtype, CUDA/driver version, GPU clocks (nvidia-smi -lgc to lock, or at least record clocks and temperature), and confirm no other tenant on the GPUs.

4. Measure the baseline as a load sweep, not a point. Ramp QPS in steps, hold each step for at least 5 minutes after a warmup discard of the first 60 s, and record TTFT and TPOT percentiles per step. The output is a curve of tok/s vs p99 latency; the operating point is where the curve knees.

5. Instrument the mechanism, not just the outcome. Collect achieved HBM bandwidth, SM occupancy, KV blocks used/total, preemption and swap counters, and queue depth. Without these you cannot distinguish "helped" from "helped because it accidentally shortened outputs".

6. Repeat. At least 3 independent runs per arm, interleaved (A B A B) to absorb thermal and neighbour drift. Report median and spread; a single run difference under ~5% is noise on shared hardware.

Boundary condition: this plan measures steady state only. It says nothing about cold start, weight-load time, or recovery after an OOM, which need separate tests.

Falsifiable hypothesis: the change increases sustained tok/s at the SLO-constrained operating point by more than the run-to-run spread. If the gain is within spread, the answer is "no measurable effect", not "small improvement".

Rollback gate: ship only if the interleaved runs show a gain exceeding 2x the observed run-to-run standard deviation, with zero preemptions and no p99 regression; otherwise revert and keep the baseline config.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether decode helps a serving workload. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Goal: validate whether decode-side changes help, with an explicit separation of measured facts from estimates. Assumption: closed-loop and open-loop clients give different answers, so the client model must be chosen deliberately.

1. Choose the load model first. A closed-loop client with N fixed workers cannot show queueing collapse - it self-throttles, and its "latency" is really service time. Use an open-loop / constant-arrival-rate client (Poisson arrivals at target QPS) to expose queueing, and state which was used. This single choice explains most contradictory benchmark results.

2. Separate the two SLIs. TTFT is a prefill property; TPOT is a decode property. Report them independently plus end-to-end. A change that improves aggregate tok/s by batching more aggressively will usually trade TTFT for TPOT or vice versa, and a single blended number hides that.

3. Define the estimate vs measurement boundary. Measured: latency percentiles, tokens emitted, GPU counters. Estimated: cost per million tokens, headroom, projected capacity. Label them separately in the report; do not present a projection as an observation.

4. Establish a hardware ceiling before tuning software. Run a microbenchmark of achieved HBM bandwidth and compute the theoretical minimum TPOT = weight_bytes / achieved_BW for the model and dtype. If measured single-stream TPOT is already within ~20% of that floor, no scheduler tuning will help and the only remaining levers are quantization, TP, or speculative decoding. This step prevents weeks of pointless tuning.

5. Run the sweep. QPS ladder, >= 5 min per step, warmup discarded, 3 interleaved repeats per arm, identical trace replayed from a fixed seed.

6. Cross-check the counters. Confirm output token counts match between arms; a "faster" configuration that emitted fewer tokens (early EOS, truncation, different sampling seed) is a bug, not a win.

Boundary condition: results are valid only for the measured length distribution and hardware; extrapolating to longer contexts is an estimate requiring its own run, because KV pressure is nonlinear.

Falsifiable hypothesis: at matched p99 TPOT the treatment arm sustains higher QPS than baseline, and the mechanism counters (KV utilization, achieved bandwidth) move in the predicted direction. If throughput improves but no mechanism counter moves, suspect a measurement artifact.

Rollback gate: revert if token-count parity fails, if any percentile SLO is breached, or if the gain does not reproduce across all 3 interleaved repeats.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether decode helps a serving workload. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Goal: measurement plan for a decode-path change, structured so that a negative result is as informative as a positive one. Assumption: change is deployable behind a flag and revertible within one deploy cycle.

Stage 0 - hypothesis and predicted mechanism. Write down, before measuring, which counter must move and by how much. Example: "raising max_num_seqs from 16 to 32 will raise KV utilization from ~50% to ~90% and tok/s by ~1.6x, with p99 TPOT rising less than 25%." A prediction that cannot fail is not a hypothesis.

Stage 1 - offline replay. Fixed trace, fixed seed, isolated GPUs, engine and model hash pinned. Sweep QPS, 5 min per step, discard 60 s warmup, 3 interleaved repeats. Primary output: tok/s vs p99 TPOT curve per arm.

Stage 2 - mechanism verification. Confirm the predicted counters moved: KV blocks used/total, preemption and swap counts, achieved HBM GB/s, scheduler queue depth, batch-size histogram. If throughput improved but the batch-size histogram is unchanged, the causal story is wrong and the result should not be trusted even if favourable.

Stage 3 - shadow / canary. Mirror a small fraction of live traffic (or route 5% of real traffic) to the treatment arm for at least one full diurnal cycle. Production traffic has length-distribution tails and burstiness the replay trace under-represents; KV exhaustion is a tail phenomenon.

Stage 4 - failure-path testing. Deliberately drive the arm past capacity and observe behaviour: does it queue gracefully, preempt, or OOM? Record time-to-recovery. A configuration that is 20% faster and fails catastrophically at 1.1x load is worse than the baseline.

Boundary condition: canary results are only valid if the canary receives representative traffic; routing by user id or region can bias the length distribution and invalidate the comparison.

Evidence required: the tok/s vs p99 curves for both arms, the counter deltas, canary percentile dashboards over >= 24 h, and the overload-test recovery times.

Rollback gate (pre-registered): auto-revert if p99 TPOT exceeds the SLO for 5 consecutive minutes, if any OOM or engine restart occurs, or if error rate rises above baseline plus 0.1 percentage points. Reverting must be a flag flip, not a redeploy.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether decode helps a serving workload. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer:
Goal: validate a decode optimization end to end, including the statistics needed to avoid fooling ourselves. Assumption: shared cluster, so run-to-run variance is nontrivial and must be quantified rather than assumed away.

1. Quantify noise before comparing arms. Run the baseline against itself twice (A vs A). The observed difference is the noise floor. Any treatment effect smaller than that floor is not a result. On shared or thermally throttled GPUs this floor is commonly several percent - large enough to swallow most claimed optimizations.

2. Control the confounders explicitly. Pin GPU clocks or record them per run; record ambient/inlet temperature or at least GPU temperature, since sustained runs throttle; verify exclusive GPU access; pin the engine commit, model weight sha256, tokenizer version, dtype, and sampling parameters. Temperature and clock drift are the most common uncontrolled variable in GPU benchmarking.

3. Match the work exactly. Same trace, same seed, and verify afterwards that both arms emitted the same total output tokens within a small tolerance. Also verify output quality did not change - for a deterministic-greedy control subset, outputs should be token-identical unless the change legitimately alters numerics (e.g. quantization), in which case a task-level eval is mandatory rather than optional.

4. Report distributions, not means. Publish p50/p90/p99/p99.9 for TTFT and TPOT plus the full latency histogram. Mean latency systematically hides the preemption and queueing behaviour that actually breaks SLOs.

5. Attribute the win. Pair the end-to-end result with a profile (nsys or engine-internal timing) showing which phase shrank. An unattributed throughput gain is a liability: it may come from a shortcut that will regress under different traffic.

Boundary condition: conclusions hold only for the tested hardware, model, dtype, and length distribution. Any of those changing invalidates the result; do not carry the number forward as a general claim.

Falsifiable hypothesis: treatment beats baseline by more than 2x the measured A/A noise floor, the profile attributes the gain to the predicted phase, and output token parity holds.

Rollback gate: revert if token parity fails, if the greedy control subset diverges without a numerics-changing justification, if the gain is inside the noise floor, or if p99.9 regresses even when p50 improves.
